title: uNogwaja and the Lion’s Well
summary: The hare shows a boastful lion his own reflection in a deep well, and frees the animals of the valley without raising a single claw.
moral: The one who laughs at a reflection may fall into the water beneath it.
attribution: A traditional Zulu tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: A hare beside a dark round well while a lion’s silhouette leans over the water

sentences.text: The lion of the valley had grown tired of hunting.
He declared that all the animals must come to his cave each morning and bow, and that he would choose one of them for his meal.
The animals were afraid, so they came, and each morning one of them did not go home.
uNogwaja the hare listened to the weeping and thought about the lion for three days.
Then he walked to the cave and bowed lower than anyone.
“Great one,” he said, “there is another lion in this valley, a larger one, and he says the water in the well belongs to him and not to you.”
The lion roared until the leaves shook.
“Show me this lion,” he demanded. uNogwaja led him to the old stone well at the edge of the grass.
The water lay still and dark at the bottom, and when the lion leaned over, a great golden face looked back at him.
“You see?”
said the hare quietly.
“He is copying you.
He is even opening his mouth the way you do.”
The lion growled, and the reflection growled.
The lion swiped at it with one paw, and the reflection swiped back, and the lion could not bear to be mocked.
He leapt into the well to teach the other lion a lesson.
There was a great splash, and a great wet roar, and then only the sound of water finding its level again. uNogwaja sat at the edge and combed his whiskers.
“A little closer,” he said to no one in particular, “is a dangerous place to stand.”
The animals came to the well at sunset and saw that the lion was gone.
The hare did not take any credit.
He only told them that a boastful lion had met a very patient one, and that from that day the well belonged to everyone.
